Random Seed and Reproducibility - Tutorial (RLT)

Ruoqing Zhu

Last Updated: October 26, 2026

Source: vignettes/articles/feature-seed.Rmd
feature-seed.Rmd

Overview

Use RLT(seed = ...) to repeat a forest fit on fixed data. Use base R’s set.seed() to repeat random steps in the wider analysis, such as data generation or a random train/test split. Keeping these two sources of randomness separate helps you check whether a change comes from fitting or from the data.

Follow Get Started to install RLT, then load the package:

library(RLT)

Generate the data once

We use the same numeric and factor predictors, continuous response, and held-out split as in the Regression Tutorial. The response depends on predictors 2 through 6 and an additional categorical effect for predictor 6, plus independent Gaussian noise. set.seed(1) repeats this data generation; the data remain fixed for all fits below.

set.seed(1)

trainn <- 80
testn <- 20
n <- trainn + testn
p <- 10
X1 <- matrix(rnorm(n * (p/2)), n, p/2)
X2 <- matrix(as.integer(runif(n * (p/2)) * 3), n, p/2)
X_numeric <- data.frame(X1, X2)
y <- 1 + rowSums(X_numeric[, 2:6]) +
  2 * (X_numeric[, p/2 + 1] %in% c(1, 2)) + rnorm(n)

X <- X_numeric
X[, (p/2 + 1):p] <- lapply(X[, (p/2 + 1):p], as.factor)

trainX <- X[1:trainn, ]
trainY <- y[1:trainn]
testX <- X[(trainn + 1):(trainn + testn), ]
testY <- y[(trainn + 1):(trainn + testn)]

Repeat a fit with the same seed

Both calls use the same data, forest settings, and explicit fitting seed. No data are regenerated between them.

fit_A <- RLT(
  trainX, trainY, model = "regression",
  ntrees = 200, mtry = p/2, nsplit = 0,
  seed = 1, ncores = 1, verbose = FALSE
)
fit_B <- RLT(
  trainX, trainY, model = "regression",
  ntrees = 200, mtry = p/2, nsplit = 0,
  seed = 1, ncores = 1, verbose = FALSE
)

pred_A <- predict(fit_A, testX)
pred_B <- predict(fit_B, testX)

list(
  Same_OOB_Predictions = isTRUE(all.equal(fit_A$Prediction, fit_B$Prediction)),
  Same_Test_Predictions = isTRUE(all.equal(pred_A$Prediction, pred_B$Prediction)),
  OOB_MSE = mean((fit_A$Prediction - trainY)^2),
  Test_MSE = mean((pred_A$Prediction - testY)^2)
)
## $Same_OOB_Predictions
## [1] TRUE
## 
## $Same_Test_Predictions
## [1] TRUE
## 
## $OOB_MSE
## [1] 3.501257
## 
## $Test_MSE
## [1] 4.124253

The two prediction comparisons should be TRUE in the same software environment. OOB MSE uses each training observation’s out-of-bag prediction, computed only from trees whose resample omitted it. Test MSE uses the 20 held-out observations.

Change only the fitting seed

The next fit changes seed while leaving the data and other settings fixed. Resampling and split-candidate selection can therefore change, so the resulting predictions may differ.

fit_C <- RLT(
  trainX, trainY, model = "regression",
  ntrees = 200, mtry = p/2, nsplit = 0,
  seed = 2, ncores = 1, verbose = FALSE
)
pred_C <- predict(fit_C, testX)

list(
  Same_Test_Predictions_As_A = isTRUE(all.equal(pred_C$Prediction, pred_A$Prediction)),
  OOB_MSE = mean((fit_C$Prediction - trainY)^2),
  Test_MSE = mean((pred_C$Prediction - testY)^2)
)
## $Same_Test_Predictions_As_A
## [1] FALSE
## 
## $OOB_MSE
## [1] 3.430922
## 
## $Test_MSE
## [1] 3.955942

Any difference here comes from fitting randomness on the same observations.

Repeat the whole analysis

Place set.seed() before the first random step when you want to repeat data generation, a random data split, and subsequent analysis together. If RLT() has no explicit seed, it draws one from R’s random number generator, so the preceding random steps also determine that seed. Supplying RLT(seed = ...) makes the fitting seed explicit even if earlier random steps change. The same distinction applies to classification and survival models.

Record the data, code, package version, and source revision as well as the seed. Fixed seeds do not establish identical numerical results across platforms, compilers, or package revisions. See matching the documentation revision for source installation details.
